claim: HCN channels are the only members of the voltage-gated ion channel superfamily in mammals that open upon hyperpolarization.
source: Hyperpolarized-activated and cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels are the only members of the voltage-gated ion channel superfamily in mammals that open upon hyperpolarization, conferring them pacemaker properties that are instrumental for rhythmic firing of cardiac and neuronal cells.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a defining characteristic of HCN channels and is part of established scientific knowledge about this channel family.

claim: Activation of HCN channel voltage-sensor domains upon hyperpolarization occurs through a downward movement of the S4 helix bearing the gating charges.
source: Activation of their voltage-sensor domains (VSD) upon hyperpolarization occurs through a downward movement of the S4 helix bearing the gating charges, which triggers a break in the alpha-helical hydrogen bonding pattern at the level of a conserved Serine residue.
evidence: This claim is supported by previous structural and molecular simulation studies as referenced in the abstract and introduction.

claim: Previous structural and molecular simulation studies had failed to capture pore opening that should be triggered by VSD activation in HCN channels.
source: Previous structural and molecular simulation studies had however failed to capture pore opening that should be triggered by VSD activation, presumably because of a low VSD/pore electromechanical coupling efficiency and the limited timescales accessible to such techniques.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous work and provides context for the current study.

claim: The electromechanical coupling mechanism in HCN1 involves reorganization of interfaces between VSD helices and pore-forming helices.
source: We propose that the coupling mechanism involves the reorganization of the interfaces between the VSD helices, in particular S4, and the pore-forming helices S5 and S6, subtly shifting the balance between hydrophobic and hydrophilic interactions in a 'domino effect' during activation and gating in this region.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the enhanced sampling MD simulations and analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Simulations reveal state-dependent occupancy of lipid molecules at the VSD-pore coupling interface.
source: Remarkably, our simulations reveal state-dependent occupancy of lipid molecules at this emergent coupling interface, suggesting a key role of lipids in hyperpolarization-dependent gating.
evidence: This is directly observed in the MD simulations as shown in Figure 5 and related analyses.

claim: HCN channels are crucial to control rhythmic activity in many cell types.
source: These channels are crucial to control the rhythmic activity in many cell types and further regulate cellular excitability in a wide range of electrically excitable cells (Brown et al., 1979; Santoro et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work establishing the physiological role of HCN channels.

claim: HCN channels have been implicated in heart arrhythmias, epilepsies, and neuropathic pain.
source: Given their ubiquity in excitable organs and unique role in electrical signaling, HCN channels have been implicated in a variety of diseases (e.g. heart arrhythmias, epilepsies, and neuropathic pain) and are considered as promising targets for the development of novel drugs (Benarroch, 2013; Biel et al., 2009; Bleakley et al., 2021; DiFrancesco and DiFrancesco, 2015; DiFrancesco et al., 2019; Oyrer et al., 2019; Tanguay et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to clinical and pharmacological studies.

claim: HCN channels form tetrameric assemblies around a central pore.
source: HCN channels are members of the voltage-gated ion channel (VGIC) superfamily, and as such form tetrameric assemblies around a central pore that opens and closes in response to changes in the transmembrane voltage.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about voltage-gated ion channels.

claim: Each HCN channel monomer is composed of six transmembrane helices divided into a voltage-sensing domain and a pore domain.
source: Each monomer is composed of six transmembrane helices divided into two domains: the voltage-sensing domain (VSD) is a four-helical bundle formed by the first four helices (S1–S4) (Long et al., 2005) while the pore domain is formed by tetramerization of the final two helices (S5 and S6) around the symmetry axis (Lu et al., 2001).
evidence: This structural organization is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: The pore gate in HCN channels is located at the C-terminus of the S6 helix.
source: HCN and other VGICs are allosteric systems where movement of gating charges in the VSD upon changes in electric field governs opening and closing of the pore gate located >10 Å away at the C-terminus of the S6 helix in a process known as electromechanical coupling (Blunck and Batulan, 2012; Long et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The polarity of electromechanical coupling in HCN channels is inverted relative to nearly all other voltage-gated ion channels.
source: Interestingly, the polarity of the coupling in HCN channels is inverted relative to nearly all other VGICs; HCN channels are opened by the downward movement of the gating charges during hyperpolarization, whereas most other channels are closed (Männikkö et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a well-established functional characteristic of HCN channels supported by citation.

claim: HCN channels adopt a non-domain swapped architecture where the VSD packs against the pore domain of the same subunit.
source: The first high-resolution structures of HCN1 revealed that, unlike canonical VGICs, HCN channels adopt a non-domain swapped architecture where the VSD packs against the pore domain of the same subunit (Lee and MacKinnon, 2017).
evidence: This is based on the cryoEM structure of HCN1 as cited.

claim: The non-domain swapped architecture is characteristic of channels containing a C-terminal cyclic nucleotide-binding domain connected to the pore via the C-linker.
source: This unusual fold is not unique to HCN channels but rather is characteristic of the subfamily of channels containing a C-terminal cyclic nucleotide-binding domain (CNBD) connected to the pore via the C-linker (James and Zagotta, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article on this channel family.

claim: HCN1 structures were obtained in resting and activated conformations of the VSD but the pore remained closed in both models.
source: HCN1 structures were obtained in resting and activated conformations of the VSD but the pore remained closed in both models (Lee and MacKinnon, 2017; Lee and MacKinnon, 2019).
evidence: This is based on the published cryoEM structures as cited.

claim: The model for VSD activation from HCN1 structures agrees with predictions from cysteine accessibility, patch-clamp fluorometry, and molecular dynamics simulations.
source: The model for VSD activation from these structures agrees with predictions from cysteine accessibility (Bell et al., 2004), patch-clamp fluorometry (Dai et al., 2019), and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations (Kasimova et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple experimental and computational studies.

claim: Structures of HCN4 have been resolved in both closed and open states with the VSD in the resting conformation in both cases.
source: Furthermore, structures of HCN4 have been resolved in both the closed and open state, but in both cases, the VSD is in the resting conformation (Saponaro et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on the published cryoEM structures of HCN4 as cited.

claim: The HCN1 and HCN4 structures represent three out of four states in a classical allosteric model of channel gating: resting-closed, activated-closed, and resting-open conformations.
source: Together, the HCN1 and HCN4 structures represent three out of the four states in a classical allosteric model of channel gating; the resting-closed, activated-closed, and resting-open conformations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the available structural data cited above.

claim: The activated-open state is missing from available HCN channel structures and is central to understanding electromechanical coupling.
source: The missing activated-open state is central to understanding the electromechanical coupling mechanism in the HCN family.
evidence: This is an inference based on the gap in available structural data.

claim: The experimentally measured coupling energy in HCN channels is 3–4.5 kcal/mol.
source: The experimentally measured coupling energy of only 3–4.5 kcal/mol indicates that activation of all four voltage sensors only increases the stability of the open pore relative to the closed pore by roughly one hydrogen bond (Ryu and Yellen, 2012).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements as cited.

claim: Activation of all four voltage sensors in HCN channels increases the stability of the open pore relative to the closed pore by roughly one hydrogen bond.
source: The experimentally measured coupling energy of only 3–4.5 kcal/mol indicates that activation of all four voltage sensors only increases the stability of the open pore relative to the closed pore by roughly one hydrogen bond (Ryu and Yellen, 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental coupling energy measurement.

claim: In the resting state, W281 is facing S1 and nestled in a hydrophobic cavity formed at the interface between S4, S1, and the HCN domain.
source: In the resting state, W281 is facing S1 and nestled in a hydrophobic cavity formed at the interface between S4, S1, and the HCN domain (Figure 1D) and remains stably bound at this position throughout the simulation (Figure 1G, blue bars).
evidence: This is observed in equilibrium MD simulations of the resting state structure and shown in Figure 1D and 1G.

claim: In the activated state, W281 is pulled out of the hydrophobic cavity and primarily interacts with lipids.
source: In the activated state, the intracellular S1-S4-S5 region becomes much less compact and W281 is pulled out of the hydrophobic cavity, disrupting all interactions with S1 (Figure 1F). A new interaction with the pore domain is formed via V296 in S5, but the overall protein contact of W281 is significantly reduced in the activated state. As a result, W281 primarily interacts with lipids (POPC) in the activated state through hydrophobic and electrostatic contacts.
evidence: This is observed in equilibrium MD simulations of the activated state structure and shown in Figure 1F and 1G.

claim: The Y289D mutant structure represents an 'intermediate state' conformation for VSD activation.
source: As a result of the mixed set of W281 contacts shared with the resting and activated states, the structure of the Y289D mutant can be described as an 'intermediate state' conformation for VSD activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of W281 contacts in MD simulations of the Y289D mutant structure.

claim: Full VSD activation occurs in only one VSD in the intact system under hyperpolarizing conditions.
source: In the intact system, full activation occurs in only one VSD as marked by movement of R267 past the charge transfer center (Figure 2A and B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is observed in MD simulations under hyperpolarizing electric field as shown in Figure 2.

claim: S4 adopts the characteristic bend associated with channel activation in subunits showing full or partial activation.
source: In the subunits showing full or partial activation, S4 adopts the characteristic bend associated with channel activation observed in our previous simulations and the cryoEM structure of the cadmium-crosslinked activated state (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is observed in the hyperpolarizing simulations and compared to previous work.

claim: The HCND-less system shows accelerated voltage sensor activation compared to the intact system.
source: For the HCND-less system, one VSD undergoes full activation while the remaining three undergo partial activation over the course of a 750 ns simulation (Figure 2D and E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B). This is consistent with an accelerated voltage sensor activation compared to the intact system expected by relieving inhibition of activation provided by the HCN domain.
evidence: This is observed by comparing simulations with and without the HCN domain.

claim: During VSD activation, downward movement of gating charges and bending of S4 is correlated with rotation of the C-terminus of S4.
source: During VSD activation, downward movement of the gating charges and bending of S4 is correlated with rotation of the C-terminus of S4, pointing W281 toward the lipid interface (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2C and F).
evidence: This correlation is observed in the hyperpolarizing MD simulations.

claim: A hydrogen bond forms between W281 and N300 in subunits undergoing complete activation.
source: In subunits undergoing complete activation, a more complete rotation of the C-terminus of S4 results in the formation of a hydrogen bond between W281 and N300 that was observed in the Y289D mutant above (Figure 2A and D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and D), consistent with equilibrium simulations of the activated state of HCN1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is observed in the hyperpolarizing simulations and is consistent with equilibrium simulations.

claim: Swapping W281 and N300 inverts the gating polarity in the related spHCN channel.
source: Interestingly, swapping these two residues inverts the gating polarity in the related spHCN channel (W355N/N370W, spHCN numbering).
evidence: This is based on previous experimental work on spHCN as referenced.

claim: Rotation of W281 is accompanied by an increase in the hydrophobic contact area at the lower S4/S5 interface.
source: In our simulations of VSD activation, rotation of W281 is accompanied by an increase in the hydrophobic contact area at the lower S4/S5 interface with little change to the electrostatic interactions (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and E), reminiscent of the behavior observed in equilibrium simulations of the resting and activated states (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is observed in the hyperpolarizing simulations and shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Separation of the S1/S4 interface is one of the first steps toward release of W281 from the hydrophobic pocket.
source: On the other hand, analysis of the lower S4-S1 interface showed a decrease in the hydrophobic contacts between S4 and S1 in most (seven out of eight) subunits (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and F). This suggests that separation of the S1/S4 interface is one of the first steps toward the release of W281 from the S1/S4/HCN domain hydrophobic pocket and enabling rotation of the C-terminus of S4.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of interface contacts during activation simulations.

claim: VSD activation exposes the VSD-pore interface to the lipid bilayer.
source: The combined bending and rotation of the lower S4 accompanies the displacement of S1 away from S4 and exposes the VSD-pore interface to the lipid bilayer.
evidence: This is observed in the hyperpolarizing simulations.

claim: An increased number of contacts between lipid tails and hydrophobic residues on S4 and S5 accompanies VSD activation.
source: As a result, an increased number of contacts between lipid tails and hydrophobic residues on S4 and S5 accompanies VSD activation (Figure 2I and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is quantified in the simulations and shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The average number of POPC carbon atoms in contact with the lower S4/S5 interface is ~24 ± 7 in the resting state versus ~40 ± 7 in the activated state.
source: The average number of POPC carbon atoms in contact with the lower S4/S5 interface is ~24 ± 7 in the resting state versus ~40 ± 7 in the activated state equilibrium simulation.
evidence: This is quantified from the equilibrium MD simulations.

claim: Lipid tails preferentially contact the VSD/pore interface in the activated state of the voltage sensor.
source: This increase in lipidic contact upon activation is preserved whether the HCN domain is present or absent. Thus, lipid tails preferentially contact the VSD/pore interface in the activated state of the voltage sensor, indicating that lipid tails may play a role in electromechanical coupling in HCN1.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of lipid contacts in different states.

claim: The pore gate remained shut throughout hyperpolarizing simulations despite strategies to accelerate activation.
source: Despite the combination of three strategies to accelerate activation, the pore gate remained shut throughout these simulations.
evidence: This is directly observed in the simulations.

claim: The closed to open pore transition for HCN1 has a time constant of ~100 ms based on allosteric models of channel gating.
source: Even in the presence of four activated voltage sensors, the closed to open pore transition for HCN1 has a time constant of ~100 ms based on allosteric models of channel gating (Altomare et al., 2001).
evidence: This is based on previous functional studies as cited.

claim: The N-terminal end of S5 is displaced during VSD activation in a movement observed in MD simulations and cryoEM structures.
source: As a result of the bending and rotation of S4 during VSD activation, the N-terminal end of S5 is displaced relative to the resting state conformation in a movement that was previously observed in MD simulations and cryoEM structures.
evidence: This is observed in the current simulations and consistent with previous work.

claim: The N-terminus of S5 is similarly displaced in the Y289D mutant cryoEM structure despite lack of VSD activation.
source: Interestingly, the N-terminus of S5 is similarly displaced in the Y289D mutant cryoEM structure despite lack of VSD activation in this channel (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the Y289D structure to the resting and activated structures.

claim: Tilted conformations of the S5 helix are observed in open-channel structures of related CNBD family channels like hERG and TAX-4.
source: These tilted conformations of the S5 helix are also observed in open-channel structures of related CNBD family channels like hERG and TAX-4 (Wang and MacKinnon, 2017; Zheng et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on comparison to published structures as cited.

claim: The tilting movement of S5 following VSD activation was proposed as a critical step in electromechanical coupling of HCN1.
source: Furthermore, this region of S5 directly contacts the S6 helix near the activation gate, thus the tilting movement of S5 following VSD activation was proposed as a critical step in the electromechanical coupling of HCN1 (Lee and MacKinnon, 2019; Kasimova et al., 2019) and experimentally shown in HCN4 (Saponaro et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by previous computational and experimental studies as cited.

claim: Tilting of S5 alters the interaction network between the S4-S5 linker and the C-linker of the channel.
source: In our simulations of the resting, activated, and intermediate (Y289D) structures above, we noted that tilting of S5 also alters the interaction network between the S4-S5 linker and the C-linker of the channel (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is observed in the equilibrium simulations and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The interaction between D290 of the S4-S5 linker and K412 of the C-linker is state-specific to both the active and intermediate states.
source: The interaction between D290 of the S4-S5 linker and K412 of the C-linker is of particular interest given the clear state-specificity to both the active and intermediate states.
evidence: This is observed in the equilibrium simulations of different states.

claim: The D290-K412 distance decreases rapidly in the first few picoseconds of simulations of the activated VSD-closed pore structure.
source: Interestingly, the D290-K412 distance in the original model of the activated VSD-closed pore conformation is close to the distance observed in the resting state structure. However, this distance decreases rapidly in the first few picoseconds of simulations of the activated VSD-closed pore structure and the resulting interaction remains stable for the majority of the trajectory (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is observed in the equilibrium simulations and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The D290-K412 interaction is involved in coupling VSD movement to gate opening through the C-linker.
source: We thus hypothesize this interaction is involved in coupling VSD movement to gate opening through the C-linker.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the state-dependent nature of the interaction observed in simulations.

claim: The D290C-K412C double mutant conducts a relatively high basal current and activates at depolarized potentials compared to HCN1-EM parent constructs.
source: The HEK cells expressing D290C-K412C double mutant in the absence of cadmium conduct a relatively high basal current and activate at depolarized potentials compared to the HCN1-EM parent constructs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is observed in electrophysiology experiments and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Much of the basal current in the D290C-K412C mutant can be blocked by application of external cesium chloride.
source: Much of this basal current can be blocked by application of external cesium chloride, indicating that the D290C-K412C mutant does not fully close even in the absence of applied cadmium (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is observed in electrophysiology experiments with cesium block.

claim: In the presence of cadmium, the basal conductance of D290C-K412C increases substantially to 0.77 ± 0.7 compared to 0.44 ± 0.4 in the absence of cadmium.
source: In HEK cells patched with 100 uM cadmium chloride in the pipette, the basal conductance increases substantially to 0.77 ± 0.7 compared to 0.44 ± 0.4 in the absence of cadmium (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is measured in electrophysiology experiments and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The voltage dependence of activation in D290C-K412C shifts by 60 mV to more positive potentials in the presence of cadmium.
source: Furthermore, the voltage dependence of activation shifts by 60 mV to more positive potentials (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is measured in electrophysiology experiments and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Crossbridging D290C and K412C preferentially stabilizes the open state of HCN1.
source: The combined increase in the basal current amplitude and rightward shift in the voltage-dependence of activation in the double cysteine mutant in the presence of cadmium strongly indicates that crossbridging these positions preferentially stabilizes the open state, in agreement with our hypothesis that the D290-K412 interaction promotes channel opening.
evidence: This is inferred from the electrophysiology data on the double cysteine mutant.

claim: Distances between V390 consistently increase upon pore opening in CNBD channels.
source: In addition, a structural comparison of pairs of closed and open structures of CNBD channels revealed that distances between V390 consistently increased upon pore opening in TAX-4; this distance increases from 10.6 to 17.2 Å (PDB IDs 6WEJ-6WEK), in CNGA1 from 9.6 to 16.4 Å (PDB IDs 7LFT-7LFW), in CNGA1/B1 from 9.8 to 15.1 Å (PDB IDs 7RH9-7RHH), in EAG/hERG from 10.7 to 17.3 Å (PDB IDs 5KL7L-5VA1), and in HCN4 from 10.5 to 15.0 Å (PDB IDs 7NP4-7NP3).
evidence: This is based on structural comparisons of published structures.

claim: ABMD simulations observed a splaying apart of the S6 helices with a hinge forming around G382.
source: During these simulations, we observed a splaying apart of the S6 helices, with a hinge forming around G382, and a rotation and slight deformation of the helix bringing V390 from a position facing the pore lumen to a position still lining the inner vestibule in the open state (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in the ABMD simulations and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pore opening in ABMD simulations is coupled to an increase in the pore radius at the V390 position and increased hydration of the pore intracellular gate.
source: This event is coupled to an increase in the pore radius at the V390 position (Figure 4B) and an increased hydration of the pore intracellular gate, enabling the conduction of several K+ ions (1–3 ion permeation events in each simulation, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is observed in the ABMD simulations and shown in Figures 4B and 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: A contact between H392 and adjacent Q398 formed during the ABMD simulation initiated in the activated/closed state.
source: The rearrangement of S6 also induced the formation of other interactions between adjacent S6 helices: in particular, a contact between H392 and adjacent Q398 formed during the ABMD simulation initiated in the activated/closed state, even though the formation of these contacts was not explicitly encouraged in the biasing simulations (Figure 4C and D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is observed in the ABMD simulations and shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The contact between positions N658-Q664 is present in the open state structure of hERG.
source: The contact between positions N658-Q664 (equivalent to H392-Q398) is also present in the open state structure of hERG (Wang and MacKinnon, 2017).
evidence: This is based on comparison to the published hERG structure.

claim: The H392-Q398 contact should be formed to induce pore widening and stabilize the open conformation in HCN1.
source: Our data also suggest that other contacts could be specifically formed in the open channel, like between E282 from S4 and R404 from the adjacent C-linker. Thus, we suggest that the H392-Q398 contact (and possibly of the other aforementioned contacts with E282 and R404) should be formed to induce pore widening and stabilize the open conformation in HCN1.
evidence: This is inferred from the ABMD simulations and comparison to related channels.

claim: The intra-subunit contact area between S6 and S5 shows a slight reinforcement in the open model.
source: Calculations of the intra-subunit contact areas between S6 (from residue 386–401) and S5 (lower segment) showed a slight reinforcement of the hydrophobic contact area in the open model and ABMD simulations of HCN1, indicating that closure/opening may be related to changes of interfaces between pore-forming helices (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is calculated from the ABMD simulations and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The adjacent S6-S6 hydrophobic interfaces are substantially weakened during pore opening.
source: By contrast, the adjacent S6-S6 hydrophobic interfaces are substantially weakened, suggesting that the enlargement of the pore radius requires an increased distance between S6 helices (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is calculated from the ABMD simulations and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Formation of specific interactions between polar/charged residues at the S4/S5/S6 interface accompany pore opening.
source: In addition, the formation of specific interactions between polar/charged residues at the S4/S5/S6 interface accompany pore opening, most notably between R297 (S5) and E282 (S4) and between R297 (S5) and H392 (S6), which is coupled to a loss of contact of interactions between R297 and lipid headgroups (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is observed in the ABMD simulations and shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: A specific interaction between E282 (S4) and R404 (C-linker) appears important to stabilize the open state.
source: On top of this, a specific interaction between E282 (S4) and R404 (C-linker) appears important to stabilize the open state (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is observed in the ABMD simulations and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Lipids bind in two separate sites (sites A and B) on opposite sides of the S4/S5/S6 interface.
source: The analysis of the interaction between lipid headgroups of the lower leaflet POPC lipids and the innermost S4/S5/S6 region also revealed a state-dependent pattern (Figure 5A). Indeed, lipids tended to bind in two separate sites (sites A and B, Figure 5B and C), located on opposite sides of the S4/S5/S6 interface.
evidence: This is observed in the simulations and shown in Figure 5.

claim: In both lipid binding sites, contacts with polar or charged residues were increased in the activated state relative to the resting one.
source: In both of these sites, contacts with polar or charged residues were increased in the activated state relative to the resting one and involved a larger number of lipids.
evidence: This is observed in the analysis of lipid contacts across different states.

claim: Site B specifically engaged VSD residues, including S4 gating charges.
source: Site B specifically engaged VSD residues, including S4 gating charges.
evidence: This is observed in the analysis of lipid binding sites.

claim: Site A engaged residues on S5 (R297) and on S6 (H392).
source: Site A, located on the opposite side of the VSD/pore interface, on the other hand, engaged in addition residues on S5 (R297) and on S6 (H392).
evidence: This is observed in the analysis of lipid binding sites.

claim: R297 interacted strongly with POPC headgroups in the resting state, substantially less in the activated/closed state and almost lost all contacts in the activated/open state.
source: During pore opening in the ABMD simulations initiated in the activated state, the interactions between the innermost S4/S5/S6 region and lipid headgroups remained largely identical to those pinpointed in the activated state. The only large reduction in interaction concerned R297, which interacted strongly with POPC headgroups in the resting state, substantially less in the activated/closed state and almost lost all contacts in the activated/open state.
evidence: This is observed in the analysis of lipid contacts across different states.

claim: H392 is highly conserved in the HCN family.
source: Interestingly, H392, pinpointed as crucial for pore gating above, is located in the middle of the sequence corresponding to the inner constriction on S6 and is highly conserved in the HCN family.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and knowledge of the HCN family.

claim: H392 is capable of making contacts both with R297 on S5 and with a POPC headgroup from the lower bilayer leaflet.
source: Its position at the lipid interface allows it to be flexible. Thus, this residue is capable of making contacts both with R297 on S5, and with a POPC headgroup from the lower bilayer leaflet (Figure 5), sometimes engaging in a ternary interaction with both binding partners.
evidence: This is observed in the simulations and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Both the H392-R297 contact and the contact between H392 and lipid headgroups are reinforced in the activated state.
source: In fact, both the H392-R297 contact and the contact between H392 and lipid headgroups are reinforced in the activated state, while the contact between H392 and lipids is again broken in the open state, confirming that these contacts are likely involved in activation and opening (Figures 4E and 5).
evidence: This is observed in the analysis of contacts across different states.

claim: Lipids play a particular role in coupling S5 and S6 in a way as to enable pore gating.
source: We hypothesize that these lipids play a particular role in coupling S5 and S6 in a way as to enable pore gating.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed state-dependent lipid interactions.

claim: Activation and opening of HCN1 are driven by a combination of hydrophobic forces reinforcing the intra-subunit S4/S5/S6 interface and positioning of lipid headgroups in contact with hydrophilic residues.
source: Overall, these observations imply that activation and following opening of HCN1 are also driven by a combination of forces: on the one hand, hydrophobic forces reinforce the intra-subunit S4/S5/S6 interface, while on the other hand, the positioning of lipid headgroups in contact with hydrophilic residues located at this interface also guides the positioning of lipid tails that contribute to the overall hydrophobic region.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of interfaces and lipid interactions.

claim: Hyperpolarization triggers the downward and breaking movement of S4 at S272 and initiates a cascade of rearrangements of the hydrophobic interfaces.
source: Hyperpolarization triggers the downward and breaking movement of S4 at S272 and initiates a cascade of rearrangements of the hydrophobic interfaces between and within the voltage-sensor domains (VSD) and pore.
evidence: This is the proposed model based on the simulation results and shown in Figure 6.

claim: W281 is pulled out of a S1/HCND hydrophobic cavity leading the lower S4 helix to rotate and form new contacts with N300 on S5.
source: First, W281 is pulled out of a S1/HCND hydrophobic cavity leading the lower S4 helix to rotate and form of new contacts with N300 on S5 (step 1).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model shown in Figure 6 based on simulation results.

claim: The two-step-activation mechanism induces an increase in the hydrophobic interface between the lower S4, S5, and the surrounding lipid tails.
source: This two-step-activation mechanism induces an increase in the hydrophobic interface between the lower S4, S5, and the surrounding lipid tails, thus reinforcing coupling between the VSD and pore as S4 activates.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model shown in Figure 6 based on simulation results.

claim: The increased S4/S5 coupling and formation of the D290-K412 contact results in a slight bending of S5 away from S6.
source: The increased S4/S5 coupling as S4 is displaced from the resting state and the formation of the D290-K412 contact between the S4-S5 linker and the C-linker results in a slight bending of S5 away from S6 (Figure 6; step 2) and enables S6 to rotate radially away from the pore axis by hinging at the level of G382 to maintain and even strengthen hydrophobic S5/S6 contacts (Figure 6; step 3).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model shown in Figure 6 based on simulation results.

claim: Rotation of S6 results in an expansion of the pore via the reorientation of V390 away from the pore axis.
source: Rotation of S6 results in an expansion of the pore via the reorientation of V390 away from the pore axis and into a pore-lining position permitting conduction through the open pore.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model shown in Figure 6 based on simulation results.

claim: A two-step mechanism for VSD activation was recently identified in spHCN using VCF and gating currents.
source: A two-step mechanism for VSD activation was recently identified in spHCN using VCF and gating currents to track voltage sensor movement on the E356A (Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on recent experimental work as cited.

claim: The secondary movement of the voltage sensor in spHCN may correspond to either the bending or rotation of the lower S4 helix.
source: This mutant uncouples the primary gating charge movement from pore opening and reveals a secondary movement of the voltage sensor that correlates with channel opening. This secondary movement may correspond to either the bending or rotation of the lower S4 helix.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental observations in spHCN.

claim: Rotation of S4 alone can drive pore opening as the W281-N300 contact is formed but no bend is observed in S4 in the Y289D mutant.
source: However, our simulation of the structure of the Y289D uncoupling mutant would suggest that rotation of S4 alone can drive pore opening as the W281-N300 contact is formed but no bend is observed in S4, consistent with the model proposed by the Larsson lab (Ramentol et al., 2020).
evidence: This is inferred from the simulations of the Y289D mutant.

claim: The model for an altered S4/S5 interface upon rotation of the lower S4 explains how voltage sensor movement can still be coupled to pore gating in channels lacking a covalent linkage between the S4 and S5.
source: Furthermore, this model for an altered S4/S5 interface upon rotation of the lower S4 also explains how voltage sensor movement can still be coupled to pore gating in channels lacking a covalent linkage between the S4 and S5 (Flynn and Zagotta, 2018).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current model to previous experimental observations.

claim: Flynn and Zagotta suggested that the lower S4-S5 interface plays a critical role in stabilizing the closed state of the pore.
source: Based on their work with such split channels and extensive mutagenesis, Flynn and Zagotta suggested that the lower S4-S5 interface plays a critical role in stabilizing the closed state of the pore (Flynn and Zagotta, 2018).
evidence: This is based on previous experimental work as cited.

claim: Pore opening involves a tradeoff between a strengthening of the S5/S6 interface at the expense of a weakening of the S6-S6 interface.
source: Our simulations reveal that pore opening involves a tradeoff between a strengthening of the S5/S6 interface at the expense of a weakening of the S6-S6 interface.
evidence: This is observed in the ABMD simulations.

claim: Disruption of the leucine zipper motif between S5 and S6 reduces the ability of the VSD to drive pore opening.
source: This is consistent with previous mutagenesis of a leucine zipper motif between S5 and S6, which demonstrated that disruption of this motif reduces the ability of the VSD to drive pore opening (Wemhöner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on previous experimental work as cited.

claim: Voltage sensor activation displaces the lower S4/S5 interface away from the closed conformation of S6, enabling dilation of the S6 helices.
source: Voltage sensor activation displaces the lower S4/S5 interface away from the closed conformation of S6, enabling dilation of the S6 helices. Thus, the resting conformation of S5 sterically hinders this outward and rotating movement of S6, in line with previous studies (Flynn and Zagotta, 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the simulations and consistent with previous work.

claim: Truncation studies show the C-linker and CNBD are not necessary for channel activation.
source: Truncation studies show the C-linker and CNBD are not necessary for channel activation, but mutagenesis studies have highlighted numerous interactions between the S4-S5 linker and C-terminus critical for electromechanical coupling (Wainger et al., 2001; Decher et al., 2004; Kwan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on previous experimental studies as cited.

claim: The ABMD open state models show excellent overall agreement with cysteine crosslinking experiments from Kwan et al., 2012.
source: Highlighting these interaction pairs by their functional effect on channel gating in our ABMD open state models shows excellent overall agreement. The closest pairs of residues in our model correspond to the pairs identified to favor the open state while the more distant pairs favor the closed state or are not responsive to cadmium (Videos 1–6).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the ABMD models to previous experimental data.

claim: The open state model involves a dilation at position 390 coupled to a rotation of V390 away from the central pore axis.
source: The open state model resulting from our ABMD simulation protocol involves a dilation at position 390 coupled to a rotation of V390 away from the central pore axis, resulting from bending of S6 at the upper glycine G382.
evidence: This is observed in the ABMD simulations.

claim: V390 still lines the inner vestibule in the open state, consistent with the observation that this position influences the apparent affinity of open pore blockers.
source: The degree of rotation is low enough that V390 still lines the inner vestibule in the open state, consistent with the observation that this position influences the apparent affinity of open pore blockers (Cheng et al., 2007).
evidence: This is inferred from the ABMD simulations and consistent with previous experimental observations.

claim: Pore opening in HCN1 is coupled to deformation of the S6 helix and the formation of a π helix in several subunits.
source: Pore opening is coupled to deformation of the S6 helix and the formation of a π helix in several subunits.
evidence: This is observed in the ABMD simulations.

claim: hERG is the only channel of the CNBD family for which the transition to π helix occurs in S6.
source: Interestingly, hERG is the only channel of the CNBD family for which the transition to π helix occurs in S6.
evidence: This is based on comparison to published structures of CNBD family channels.

claim: Other CNBD family members, such as CNG channels, TAX-4, and HCN4, open via a more canonical right-handed twist of S6 at glycine 399.
source: Other CNBD family members, such as CNG channels, TAX-4, and HCN4, open via a more canonical right-handed twist of S6 at glycine 399 (Zheng et al., 2020; Xue et al., 2021; Xue et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on published structures as cited.

claim: HCN1 may feature an opening mechanism that combines features of the CNBD family and those specific to hERG opening.
source: HCN1 may thus feature an opening mechanism that combines features of the CNBD family and those specific to hERG opening.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed features in the ABMD simulations.

claim: In the HCN4 structure, the equivalent of V390 (I511) is rotated slightly but does not induce formation of a π-helix.
source: Notably, in the closest homolog of resolved open structure, HCN4, the equivalent of V390 (I511), is rotated slightly but does not induce formation of a π-helix (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on comparison to the HCN4 structure.

claim: The difference between the HCN4 cryoEM structure and simulations of HCN1 may stem from the different functional states these models represent.
source: Although it is possible that the difference observed between the HCN4 cryoEM structure and our simulations of HCN1 represents differences between isoforms, we suggest that this difference may also stem from the different functional states these models represent.
evidence: This is speculation about the differences between HCN1 and HCN4 structures.

claim: The HCN4 structure was solved in the resting VSD conformation, corresponding to the resting-open state or the 'instantaneous' open state.
source: The HCN4 structure was solved in the resting VSD conformation, thus corresponding to the resting-open state or the 'instantaneous' open state of HCN channels.
evidence: This is based on the published HCN4 structure.

claim: The instantaneous open state is pharmacologically distinguishable from the activated-open state.
source: The instantaneous open state is pharmacologically distinguishable from the activated-open state suggesting structural differences in the pore (Proenza et al., 2002).
evidence: This is based on previous experimental work as cited.

claim: Saponaro et al. report state-dependent lipid binding at the S4/S5/S6 interface in closed and open structures of HCN4.
source: Saponaro et al. also report state-dependent lipid binding at the S4/S5/S6 interface in their closed and open structures of HCN4, though they observe lipid density only in the resting-closed state and not in the resting-open state (Saponaro et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on the published HCN4 structures as cited.

claim: A similar lipid density was observed in the resting-closed structure of the hyperpolarization-activated plant channel KAT1.
source: A similar lipid density was observed in the resting-closed structure of the hyperpolarization-activated plant channel KAT1 (Clark et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on the published KAT1 structure as cited.

claim: A recent study proposed a mechanism for the regulation of SthK by PA lipids.
source: Strikingly, a recent study reported recording from the related bacterial channel SthK in bilayers of controlled lipid composition and proposed a mechanism for the regulation of this channel by PA lipids (Schmidpeter et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on a recent study as cited.

claim: CryoEM structures of SthK showed lipid binding to a site containing residues corresponding to R297 and D401 engaged in a salt bridge interaction in the closed state.
source: Indeed, cryoEM structures of this channel in different states where individual lipid molecules were resolved and showed lipid binding to a site containing residues corresponding to R297 and D401 engaged in a salt bridge interaction in the closed state of SthK (HCN1 numbering).
evidence: This is based on the published SthK structures.

claim: The lipid is absent in the open state of SthK, and the R297-D401 salt bridge is also broken.
source: This lipid is absent in the open state, and the aforementioned salt bridge is also broken, leading the authors to propose that PA acts in an activatory manner via an unlocking mechanism by binding in the closed state.
evidence: This is based on the published SthK structures and proposed mechanism.

claim: Mutagenesis of the equivalent positions in HCN2 confirmed that the PA regulation mechanism is likely conserved in HCN.
source: Mutagenesis of the equivalent positions in HCN2 confirmed that this mechanism is likely conserved in HCN.
evidence: This is based on experimental work on HCN2 as referenced in the SthK study.

claim: HCN1 opening simulations reveal reduced contacts between R297 and D401 and lipid headgroups in the activated/closed and activated/open states compared to the resting/closed state.
source: Consistent with this model, our HCN1 opening simulations reveal reduced contacts between R297 and D401 and lipid headgroups in the activated/closed and in the activated/open state compared to the resting/closed state (Figure 5).
evidence: This is observed in the simulations and shown in Figure 5.
